transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-07 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees (Redwood): Liam Chen, Marisol Vega, Sanjay Rao, Ava Martinez
Attendees (Customer): Priya Nair, Ethan Brooks, Dara Kim, Marcus Lee
Links referenced: perf-traces.s3://redwood-omni/2026-11-07, doc: redwood/benchmarks/mixed-gpu-template.xlsx, drive: https://drive.redwood.com/omni/pilot-plan

[00:00] Liam Chen: Hey everyone, uh thanks for carving out time. we wanted to dig in on the mixed GPU behavior you saw in the pilot, specifically the cuda graph replay instability when the KV cache is warm. quick round of intros?

[00:22] Priya Nair: Priya here, we run the inference infra for OmniRetail, running a mixed fleet of A100s and a handful of H100s in the same rack, NVLink zones partially connected. we saw spikes and sometimes the process falls back and throughput drops by 30%.

[00:40] Marisol Vega: ok, thanks. quick clarification — when you say falls back, is that the runtime choosing a different kernel path, or are you seeing a CUDA error and then a fallback to CPU?

[00:52] Ethan Brooks: No CPU fallback. it's the GPU kernel path switching, like the TensorRT LLM path versus the PyTorch/Triton path. sometimes cudagraph replay gives wrong stream ordering and the kernel selector reverts to a conservative execpath.

[01:10] Sanjay Rao: that matches tickets we've looked at — mixed SM capability plus NVLink topology can influence launch heuristics, especially with persistent KV and prefetched embeddings in L2. Curious about sequence lengths and batching pattern?

[01:28] Dara Kim: Our traffic is mixed: 20% long (2k tokens), 60% medium (512), 20% short (64). steady QPS ~1800 but bursts up to 3k. we use a persistent KV cache to reduce token compute for medium/short flows.

[01:45] Ava Martinez: noted. can you confirm quantization settings? FP16 or FP8? we saw different behaviors if the kernel uses TF32/FP16 vs the newer FP8 kernels — FP8 kernels can be faster but more fragile on heterogeneous fleets.

[02:03] Priya Nair: currently FP16 for PyTorch runtime; we enabled an experimental FP8 flag on TRT-LLM on the H100s for pilot but left A100s on FP16.

[02:15] Marisol Vega: that mix is a likely suspect. TRT-LLM will pick FP8-optimized kernels on H100 which assume certain tensor core behaviors. when you have sequences primed in KV and then a cudagraph replay that doesn't capture dynamic mem offsets, you can get misaligned launches and then the runtime falls back to a safer, slower kernel.

[02:36] Marcus Lee: from a security/compliance angle, we need to keep everything inside our VPC and use customer-managed KMS for keys. if we move to a private deployment we'll need audit logs for kernel-level traces — is that supported?

[02:49] Liam Chen: yes, private supports sys-level NVTX traces archived to S3 with RBAC. we'll share docs. but wanted to continue on perf — Marisol, can you run through what traces we should collect for a reproducible triage?

[03:05] Marisol Vega: absolutely. the minimal set: NVTX timeline, per-kernel launch times, CUDA graph capture/replay IDs, cublas/cuops logs, and the runtime's kernel-selector diagnostic dump. also a short sample corpus capturing warm and cold cache runs. ideally three runs per config: cold KV (empty), warm KV (steady traffic), and primed KV (aggressive prefetch).

[03:30] Ethan Brooks: we have NVTX already for a few runs. we can run the warm/cold sets. how do we instrument cudagraph replay points to correlate with kernel switch?

[03:41] Sanjay Rao: insert NVTX ranges around the capture and replay calls; capture the graph id and attach it to the trace. also enable stream priority profiling so we can see if stream contention triggers an alternate path.

[03:56] Dara Kim: question — what about NUMA and PCIe locality? we have a mix of PCIe-connected H100 and NVLink A100 pairs in the same node, but affinity is not uniform. could that cause the kernel selector to behave differently?

[04:10] Marisol Vega: yes, NUMA matters. if memory addresses for KV pages live on a device not local to the kernel launch, drivers may force a memcpy or cause different launch parameters. test with 'numactl --cpunodebind' and monitor page migration. also check multi-GPU kernel variants — some kernels require symmetric NVLink topologies to use fast allreduce primitives.

[04:34] Liam Chen: okay, let's walk through a live snippet from one of your traces (Priya uploaded trace #3).

[04:42] Priya Nair: yep, so in trace-3 we see a normal latency curve until minute 12, then a sudden drop in throughput and increased p99. nvtx shows a cudagraph replay at t=12:04. after that, kernel A (fast fp8 kernel) fails selection and kernel B (conservative fp16 kernel) is used.

[05:05] Marisol Vega: can you read out the exact cuda error or is it just a selector log?

[05:10] Priya Nair: selector log: "kernel path invalidated: cudagraph mismatch at offset 0x3f4" and then runtime: "fallback to slow_path_v2" — no device-side exception thrown though.

(Note: The above line duplicated by mistake, continuing real transcript)

[05:18] Marisol Vega: that "cudagraph mismatch" text is consistent with a capture that assumed a static offset for the KV cache buffer but later the buffer was relocated or had different alignment because of a different allocator path — happens if PyTorch caching allocator behaves differently across runs. TRT's graph capture can be brittle to that.

[05:35] Ethan Brooks: so would switching to unified allocator or pinning addresses help?

[05:40] Marisol Vega: pinning does help. also capturing graphs after the allocation state stabilizes, and using our runtime's graph replay shim which validates offsets at replay time and triggers a controlled re-capture if mismatch detected. that re-capture is better than silent fallback.

[05:56] Sanjay Rao: we should also consider kernel eviction due to memory fragmentation. long-lived KV cache consumes big chunks, and combined with dynamic batch allocation you can fragment memory, causing the selector to avoid large fast kernels despite presence of free memory.

[06:12] Dara Kim: how do we quantify fragmentation? any counters or metrics we can emit?

[06:17] Ava Martinez: emit free-block histograms (our runtime already exposes hole sizes), page migration rates, and nvml memory allocation equality. correlate with cudagraph capture timestamps. we can add a short utility to take a 'heap map' snapshot around captures.

[06:32] Priya Nair: on quantization — we enabled FP8 on H100s only for TRT and left PyTorch on FP16. would a consistent quant mode across fleet reduce selectors switching?

[06:45] Marisol Vega: absolutely. mixing quantization modes changes which kernels are valid. kernel selection usually looks at dtype + tensor shape + device compute capability. mixed dtype across devices can cause cross-device fallbacks unless the routing layer pins requests to specific device classes.

[07:00] Liam Chen: this brings up routing — are you currently routing by SKU?

[07:05] Priya Nair: partial. routing is probabilistic; we send to any available GPU in the pool to maximize utilization. but we can mark traffic as H100-prefer if needed.

[07:12] Marisol Vega: for pilot, recommend deterministic routing by SKU for the TRT FP8 path. that reduces variance and helps isolate whether the fallback is topology-induced or kernel mismatch-induced.

[07:25] Ethan Brooks: ok will try that. question about cudagraph capture strategy: do you recommend one graph per batch size, or dynamic graphs per sequence length bucket?

[07:36] Marisol Vega: we usually capture per common batch/seq bucket. capturing too many graphs increases overhead and is brittle. we recommend buckets: short(<=64), medium(128-512), long(>512) and special graph for priming/kv-heavy flows.

[07:50] Sanjay Rao: also tune graph replay TPU-like? sorry, I meant tune stream priorities and ensure the capture/replay uses a dedicated stream. avoid reusing streams with different priority during replay.

[08:05] Marcus Lee: security question — traces will contain some prompt metadata. can we mask or redact before sharing?

[08:12] Liam Chen: yes, we have an automated redaction pipeline; we'll only ask for structural trace data plus hashed prompt IDs. full prompt content stays inside Omni's bucket.

[08:22] Priya Nair: good. switching back: PyTorch runtime shows fewer sudden fallbacks but higher median latency; TRT shows better median but higher volatility. is that typical?

[08:34] Marisol Vega: yes, TRT's aggressive kernel specialization gives better steady-state but it's less tolerant to layout/allocator changes. PyTorch approach is more conservative but stable. choice depends on SLOs: latency p50 vs p99 and tail behavior during bursts.

[08:50] Ava Martinez: we saw in other pilots that adding a micro-batching layer that absorbs bursts and pre-primes KV can keep TRT on its fast path while keeping p99 bounded. it's more complicated but saves cost.

[09:03] Ethan Brooks: micro-batching sounds promising but increases QPS variance. any advice on warm/cold thresholds?

[09:10] Marisol Vega: aim for a priming window that matches your typical session length: prime KV for the next N tokens observed historically. we can run an analysis on your logs to recommend N.

[09:24] Liam Chen: let's talk about fallback mitigation: 1) deterministic routing to SKU, 2) pinned allocator or graph-shim validation & re-capture, 3) heap fragmentation monitoring and small-defrag windows, 4) avoid mixing FP8/FP16 unless pinned. anything to add?

[09:44] Sanjay Rao: consider a staged rollout of FP8: start with read-only workloads, then accept small percent of traffic, watch for kernel churn. also ensure driver/runtime versions match across nodes; small driver diffs can change kernel availability.

[10:02] Dara Kim: driver versions are slightly different — H100 nodes are on 535.x but A100 on 520.x. could that explain kernel mismatch?

[10:10] Marisol Vega: yes, driver and cuBLAS versions affect which cublas kernels are chosen. align drivers or at least test with compatibility matrix. we'll share a compatibility checklist.

[10:22] Priya Nair: great. one more deep question: we noticed that when one H100 had a small temp throttle the whole rack's kernel selections changed and workloads got moved. is that due to compute capability sensing or NVLink congestion?

[10:37] Marisol Vega: both possible. thermal throttling reduces available SMs which can make certain kernels invalid due to min-SM requirements. NVLink congestion can cause slower allreduce which some kernels assume as cheap and therefore they get invalidated. monitor per-GPU occupancy and NVLink bw counters.

[10:56] Liam Chen: ok, let's switch to concrete pilot plan and required artifacts. Marisol, can you enumerate the configs to run?

[11:04] Marisol Vega: sure, minimal pilot matrix: 
- Config A: TRT-LLM on H100s (FP8 enabled), A100s offline or isolated
- Config B: TRT-LLM across mixed fleet with deterministic routing to H100 for FP8 traffic
- Config C: PyTorch runtime (FP16) across mixed fleet
- Config D: TRT with graph-shim (re-capture on mismatch) across mixed fleet
- Each config: runs for cold/warm/primed, 3 repeats, with NVTX and heap snapshots

[11:36] Ethan Brooks: timeline?

[11:38] Liam Chen: quick: capture tests by 2026-11-12, Redwood will analyze and return with triage by 2026-11-15, pilot kickoff/infra changes 2026-11-18.

[11:50] Priya Nair: ok we can do that.

[11:53] Marisol Vega: last thing — we'll also check kernel selector logs to see if the selector is making decisions due to "tensor alignment" vs "sm_count" vs "bandwidth hint". those three flags tell a lot.

[12:06] Liam Chen: perfect. any final questions before we wrap?

[12:12] Marcus Lee: stateful logs and redaction — we'll require a join on the audit format. Liam you'll send template?

[12:18] Liam Chen: yes, action item noted. I'll upload the template and S3 path.

[12:23] Priya Nair: thanks all, this was super helpful.

[12:27] Liam Chen: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the benchmark matrix and keep the NVTX traces private.

[12:32] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: Some auto-generated labels and transcriptions may be imperfect. Technical terms sometimes mis-identified (e.g., "graph-shim" may appear as "grab shim" in raw auto text). The diagnostic logs referenced are available in the S3 bucket for the triage team.
